findings.description: FIND: bench/evidence.py, EvidenceStore.verify_bundle(). The function verifies only paired items from `zip(bundle.records, bundle.inclusion_proofs)` and never checks that the two lists have equal length. Evidence: Python zip truncates to the shorter list. A malformed bundle with extra records or extra proofs can be reported valid as long as all zipped pairs verify.

FIND — `export_bundle` computes the Merkle root from the latest epoch when epochs exist, but builds inclusion proofs from `build_inclusion_proof()` which always computes the root over ALL current records. If additional records were appended after the last epoch was sealed, the epoch's `merkle_root` covers only `record_count` records while the proof was built against the full set. The proof will not verify against the epoch root. This breaks bundle verification on the happy path whenever unsealed records exist beyond the last epoch boundary.

FOLLOW: `verify_bundle` passes `bundle.merkle_root` (the epoch root) to `verify_inclusion_proof`, which checks `proof["merkle_root"] != merkle_root`. Since `build_inclusion_proof` embeds the full-chain root and the bundle stores the epoch root, the embedded root check fails → `verify_inclusion_proof` returns `False` → every proof in the bundle is reported invalid. The entire evidence bundle feature is broken for any chain with post-epoch records.
findings.proposed_fix:
In `export_bundle`, do not use the epoch root. Compute the Merkle root from the same leaf set used by `build_inclusion_proof` (all records):
# Replace the epoch-based root selection with:
leaves = [_digest_bytes(r["chain_hash"]) for r in raw_records]
merkle_root = "sha256:" + rfc9162_merkle_root(leaves).hex()
This ensures the bundle root always matches the proofs. Alternatively, build proofs against the epoch leaf subset, but that requires knowing which epoch each record belongs to — more complexity for no gain at PoC stage.

findings.description:
FIND — `_classify_event` uses string containment (`f"CONFIRM {finding_id}" in payload_str`) on the full JSON-dumped payload. This produces false positives when one finding ID is a substring of another in the JSON structure. E.g., if `payload_str` contains `"CONFIRM C0001 and C0002"` and we're classifying for `C0002`, the search for `"CONFIRM C0002"` matches — but so does a search for `C0001` on the same record, which might find `"CONFIRM C0001"` and classify it as "confirmed" for C0001 even though the actual verdict was on both. More critically: `json.dumps` on the payload means the search matches across key names, not just verdict text. A metadata key like `"CONFIRM_TEMPLATE"` adjacent to the finding ID could trigger a false match.

FOLLOW: False classification means provenance traces show incorrect event types. A finding could appear "confirmed" when it was actually just "submitted" with a reference to CONFIRM in an unrelated context. This produces misleading provenance for the human reviewer.
findings.proposed_fix: At PoC stage, the risk is low because verdict strings follow a rigid format in practice. Accept as-is with a comment noting the limitation, or tighten with a regex: `re.search(rf'\bCONFIRM\s+{re.escape(finding_id)}\b', payload_str)`. The regex approach is one line and eliminates the substring problem.

findings.description:
FIND — `_extract_finding_ids` regex `r"\bC\d{4}\b"` requires exactly 4 digits. If finding IDs ever use 5+ digits (C10000+) or fewer (C001), they are silently missed. The `\b` word boundary also means finding IDs embedded without whitespace separation (e.g., `"C0001/C0002"`) would still match because `/` is a word boundary — this is actually fine. But IDs at start/end of strings are also fine due to `\b`. The real issue is the fixed 4-digit width.

FOLLOW: At PoC scale with <100 findings, this is not triggered. Only relevant if the system scales beyond 9999 findings.
findings.proposed_fix: No fix needed at PoC stage. The 4-digit format is the canonical ID format per the communication protocol (`C0001`, `C0002`). Document the assumption.
